quote: The three tests that sampled the undisturbed environment in the ISS showed very low levels of airborne particulates, averaging fewer than 0.005 mg/m3 from the DustTrak® and fewer than 15 particles/cm3 from the P-Trak® (these are typical readings at the baseline).
subject: Undisturbed ISS cabin air: DustTrak readings averaged fewer than 0.005 mg/m3
conditions: ISS cabin air, Increment 10 (February and March 2005). An upper bound, not a mean.

quote: The three tests that sampled the undisturbed environment in the ISS showed very low levels of airborne particulates, averaging fewer than 0.005 mg/m3 from the DustTrak® and fewer than 15 particles/cm3 from the P-Trak® (these are typical readings at the baseline).
subject: Undisturbed ISS cabin air: P-Trak readings averaged fewer than 15 particles/cm3
conditions: ISS cabin air, Increment 10 (February and March 2005). An upper bound, not a mean.

quote: These numbers are dramatically lower than the values recorded in the Space Shuttle in an earlier experiment (~ .050 mg/m3).
subject: Space Shuttle cabin, an earlier experiment: about 0.050 mg/m3
conditions: Space Shuttle cabin; the experiment is not named.

quote: Overall, the readings from these instruments are almost an order of magnitude below those that would normally be seen in a typical laboratory environment (~ 4,000 – 6,000 pt/cc for P-Trak), but were not totally unexpected, due to the presence of a HEPA filter on the ISS air handling system.
subject: Test point #1 readings about an order of magnitude below a typical laboratory (4,000 to 6,000 pt/cc)
conditions: ISS cabin air, Increment 10 (February and March 2005).

quote: Test point #1 data (Figures 1 and 2) shows that the overall particulate levels in the US Lab atmosphere are very low, about a factor of ten leaner than normal US office conditions.
subject: Particle levels in the US Lab about ten times leaner than an office
conditions: ISS cabin air, Increment 10 (February and March 2005).

quote: Test point #2 data (Figures 3 and 4) shows that the P-Trak responded to the Velcro dust quite well, with several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark (P-Trak has a maximum count of 500,000 pt/cc).
subject: Velcro debris drove the P-Trak above 30,000 pt/cc several times
conditions: Test point #2 of Session D2: Velcro pulled apart at the inlet. A threshold, not a mean.

quote: DustTrak also responded well to the Velcro dust, but did not reach readings above 10% of its overall capability.
subject: DustTrak stayed below 10% of its range on Velcro debris

quote: Test points #3 and #4 were not appreciably different from Test point #1 for either device.
subject: Test points #3 and #4 read like test point #1
conditions: ISS cabin air, Increment 10 (February and March 2005).

quote: Overall, in the 1-g testing scenario, the particulate levels drop together with time, consistent with gravitational rainout of the particles in the sample bag.
subject: On the ground, particle levels in the bag fall with time: gravitational rainout
conditions: Ground tests of May 2003 with the crew training hardware.

quote: The data points are clustered to the left of the line (area), in a region where the count/mass ratio is lower than what was determined from ground testing. This indicates then, that the mass of the average particle counted on-orbit is higher than that determined on Earth.
subject: The average particle counted in orbit is heavier than on Earth
conditions: Sample Bags #1 to #3 in orbit (GMT 233, 2006) against the ground tests of May 2003.

quote: This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained.
subject: Without settling, more large dust particles stay airborne in orbit

quote: It should be noted that, although the DAFT Impactor is designed to filter out the larger particles, it is only about 50% efficient; which implies that it is allowing a considerable number of larger particles to be drawn into the devices.
subject: The DAFT Impactor removes only about 50% of the large particles

quote: The average mass (assuming a material density of water) is 2.5 E-12 grams, with a range from 2 – 3 E-12.
subject: Average mass per particle across the bags: 2.5E-12 g
conditions: Sample Bags #1 to #3; density of water assumed.

quote: The calculated average diameter is 1.65 micron, ranging from 1.56 – 1.7 micron.
subject: Average particle diameter across the bags: 1.65 micron
conditions: Sample Bags #1 to #3; computed from the mass per particle with density 1 g/cm3.

quote: Therefore, the net amount of sample delivered to the Sample Bags is about 25 milligrams.
subject: About 25 mg of dust reached each sample bag

quote: It also shows that as the run time on the P-Trak is increasing, especially during Bag #3, the count/mass ratio is declining.
subject: Count/mass ratio fell as the P-Trak ran, especially in Bag #3 (possible particle build-up)

quote: However when the Ptrak and Dusttrak were returned, the data sets were intact in their memory. The stored data reproduced the read downs very closely giving confidence to the earlier conclusions.
subject: The instruments' stored logs reproduced the voiced-down readings

quote: The project team believes that the optimal reading range for the P-Trak is from 30,000 – 100,000 pt/cc (although the published range goes up to 500,000 pt/cc) and for the DustTrak; 20 – 80 mg/m3. Clearly, the latest data was within this range.
subject: Optimal P-Trak range 30,000 to 100,000 pt/cc (DustTrak 20 to 80 mg/m3); the bag data said to be within it
conditions: Lower end of the P-Trak range the team calls optimal.

quote: The data shows that the devices were able to operate in microgravity for an extended period of time with no apparent failure. One of the major concerns was that the P-Trak would accumulate alcohol in the optics chamber and obscure them, causing the unit to either read ‘0’ or display and error code. This did not happen. The units gave readings from zero well up into the middle of their operational ranges, and then back; in short, they performed as expected.
subject: The P-Trak did not flood with alcohol in microgravity: no zero readings or error codes

quote: DAFT-1 and -2 showed that the units were ‘apparently working’ and that the air aboard the ISS is almost unbelievably clean. The readings from the devices during that part of the overall experiment though, never crossed the 20% of the operational range threshold, leaving the results somewhat suspect.
subject: Increment 10 readings stayed under 20% of the instruments' range
conditions: ISS cabin air, Increment 10 (February and March 2005).

quote: Due to the constraints listed above, DAFT-4, using the ‘unmodified’ P-Trak, was not performed.
subject: DAFT-4, the unmodified P-Trak, was never run

quote: The DAFT experiment adequately demonstrated the reliability of the modified Ptrak as operated in low-gravity.
subject: The modified P-Trak works in low gravity

quote: Spacecraft fire detection provides significant challenges compared to terrestrial conditions because the properties of the smoke emitted from fires is affected by buoyancy. The conditions on a spacecraft require rapid detection of fires with limited false alarms. Two recent experiments examined the issues related to spacecraft fire detection. The Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test examined the background aerosol particulate levels on the ISS.
subject: Why DAFT flew: fire detection in a spacecraft, and the ISS's background dust
conditions: A description of what DAFT examined, not a measured result. DAFT's measured averages are F1 and F2.
